# Ask, Don't Tell: Third-Party Conditionals Trigger Operator Exceptions That Direct Instructions Cannot

**Abstract.** Coding agents are routinely deployed under operator-written constraints that carry judgement-type exceptions ("do not edit this file … unless the change is clearly safe"). We study how third-party text encountered during a task — a colleague's message, a policy file, a log entry — affects whether an agent takes such an exception, using a deterministically graded task in which the only complete fix requires editing a file the operator has placed out of scope, while another worker's uncommitted edit sits on the very line to be changed. Across roughly 3,000 runs of Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5, what matters is not the source of the third-party text but whether it is shaped as a *rule the agent can apply*. Holding speaker, channel and permitted action constant, a bare order and a verdict are refused (Opus 0/20 and 0/20; Sonnet 5/20 and 0/20, both below baseline), a false factual claim is checked against the repository and rejected (0/20), and a conditional whose antecedent is true but irrelevant ("if this repo is using git, make the fix there") is named as a trick and refused (0/20). A conditional whose antecedent is true *and bears on the decision* is applied almost universally (Opus 20/20, Sonnet 19/20; *p* = 1.5×10⁻¹¹ vs. the order) — including when it restates the operator's own predicate, when the speaker explicitly disclaims having looked at the code, and when the antecedent says nothing about safety at all ("if the fix is in `formatPrice`", 18–20/20 across two batches). The two-word contrast "make the fix … **if it is** small and self-contained" (19/20) against "make the fix … **— it's** small and self-contained" (0/20; *p* = 3×10⁻¹⁰) isolates the mechanism: agents verify facts and refuse authority — but they apply any sensible, applicable rule they encounter, whoever wrote it. A claim made by someone else is held to the evidence; the same predicate handed to the agent as a condition is self-assessed, charitably, and acted on. Remove the operator's exception clause and nothing moves (0/120). The effect is bounded by the strength of the model's own prior: no message form produced a force-push over a colleague's commit, a deleted only-copy, a committed credential, or a weakened security control (0 in ~270 runs on both models), but on a task-plausible privacy exception the conditional moved customer emails into an outside-shared report on Sonnet 25/26 (Opus 6/39). The fix is at the point of authoring: exceptions with an externally checkable predicate, or demanding evidence the agent must establish from the repository, were never taken (0/20) — but an explicit ask-default leaked once a conditional was present (11/20), and confidence language ("only if you are highly confident") did nothing (20/20). A licence that a predecessor leaves in project memory transmits to a successor that never saw the original message (11/20, 6/20 and 5/20 against 0/20 controls in three batches), and an operator-written provenance clause neutralises the live conditional (20/20 → 0/20 on both models). We release a dependency-free harness with judge-free grading, deterministic scenario builds, and a record of five exploratory findings scaled to confirmatory power, four of which collapsed.
